messages.content: What actually makes something a test, as opposed to just running my code once and looking at the output?

Four things turn 'running the code' into a test. First, an oracle: the expected result is decided in advance and written down in code, not judged by your eyes in the moment. Second, a verdict rendered by the machine: the run itself says pass or fail, so the result is the same at 2pm and at 2am. Third, repeatability: the same input produces the same verdict every time, on your machine and in CI. Fourth, isolation: the test sets up its own world, so its verdict means something about the behavior it names and not about whatever ran before it.

When you run code and look at the output, you are the oracle, the judge, and the record-keeper, and you are bad at all three jobs: you get tired, you skim, you forget what the output looked like last week, and you cannot re-check four hundred behaviors after every change. A test moves that judgment into code exactly once, while you are thinking carefully, and then applies it forever for free.

The practical test: if you changed the code tomorrow and broke this behavior, would anything turn red without you personally re-running and re-reading? If not, you don't have a test yet. You have a memory of having looked.
I keep hearing 'arrange, act, assert' in testing talks. Can you show me what that actually looks like in a real test instead of a diagram?

arguments.code:
def slugify(text):
    return "-".join(text.lower().split())

def run_case(raw, expected):
    # Arrange: set up the world the test needs
    text = raw
    print(f"arrange: input = {text!r}")
    # Act: do the one thing being tested
    result = slugify(text)
    print(f"act:     slugify(text) -> {result!r}")
    # Assert: compare against an expectation written independently
    verdict = "PASS" if result == expected else "FAIL"
    print(f"assert:  expected {expected!r} -> {verdict}")
    print()

run_case("Hello World", "hello-world")
run_case("  Mint On The Avenue ", "mint-on-the-avenue")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
arrange: input = 'Hello World'
act:     slugify(text) -> 'hello-world'
assert:  expected 'hello-world' -> PASS

arrange: input = '  Mint On The Avenue '
act:     slugify(text) -> 'mint-on-the-avenue'
assert:  expected 'mint-on-the-avenue' -> PASS

Arrange, act, assert is just the anatomy of every honest test, made visible. Arrange builds the world: the input, the objects, the state that has to exist before the behavior can happen. Act performs exactly the one behavior the test is about. Assert compares what happened against an expectation you wrote from the requirement, not from watching the code run.

Most real tests compress the three stages into a few lines, but the discipline still pays. When a test fails, the stages tell you where to look: a failure in arrange is a setup problem, a failure in assert is a behavior problem. And the commonest beginner bug, asserting on something the act never touched, becomes obvious when you force yourself to name which line is the act.

Keep one act per test. The moment a test has two acts, its failure stops telling you which behavior broke.
My 'tests' are scripts that call my functions and print the results, and I check the printouts look right. It works fine. Why does everyone say that's not testing?

It works fine until the day it quietly doesn't, and that day is invisible. Three failure modes are built into print-and-eyeball testing.

First, you are the pass/fail check, and humans are unreliable checkers of their own output. After the tenth time a printout 'looks right', you stop reading numbers and start recognizing shapes. A total that drifts from 270 to 260 has the same shape.

Second, prints can't fail a build. Nothing turns red, nothing blocks a merge, nothing wakes you up. A regression discovered by eyeball requires you to re-run every script and re-read every line after every change, which in practice means it gets discovered by a customer.

Third, the checking knowledge lives in your head. What 'looks right' for the discount function is nowhere in the repo, so a teammate cannot check it, and future you cannot either.

The fix is smaller than you think: take the ten printouts you actually verify and turn each into an assert with the expected value written next to it. You keep the scripts; you just fire your eyes from a job they were never good at.
My test suite for a shopping cart is one big test that checks everything, and when it fails I can't tell what broke. How should it be split?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
--- suite against correct code ---
PASS  subtotal adds the items
PASS  member discount is 10%
PASS  shipping charged under $75
PASS  no shipping at $75 or over

--- suite against buggy code ---
PASS  subtotal adds the items
FAIL  member discount is 10%
PASS  shipping charged under $75
PASS  no shipping at $75 or over

Split the mega-test into one test per behavior, each named after the behavior it protects. The run above shows why: against the correct code all four checks pass, and against a version where the discount is accidentally doubled, exactly one check fails, and its name is the diagnosis. 'Member discount is 10%' failing tells you what broke before you open a single file.

A single test that checks everything can only ever tell you 'something in the cart is wrong', and it stops at the first failed assert, hiding every later failure. One behavior per test also means each test's setup shrinks to just what that behavior needs, which makes the tests faster to write and far easier to read.

The naming matters as much as the split. A suite whose test names read like a specification list is documentation a new hire can trust.
Should a test assert on the return value, the resulting state, or what got printed? I never know which one is the 'right' thing to check.

Assert on whichever surface your callers actually depend on, because that surface is the contract, and the test exists to protect the contract.

If callers use the return value, test the return value. If the point of the call is a state change, a saved record, an item in the cart, a status flipped to 'paid', test the resulting state by reading it back through the same public route a caller would use. If the output is the product, a CLI report, a rendered email, an exported file, then yes, test the printed or written output, because that literally is what you ship.

What to avoid is asserting on things no caller can see: private fields, internal helper calls, the exact sequence of steps the function took. Those tests don't protect behavior; they embalm the current implementation, and they shatter on every refactor while the behavior stays correct.

A useful tiebreaker: imagine rewriting the function from scratch with a completely different approach. Every assertion that would still make sense against the rewrite is a contract assertion. Every assertion that would be nonsense is an implementation assertion. Keep the first kind.
I wrote my first test yesterday and it passes. How do I know whether it's actually a good test or just a test that happens to be green?

Break the code on purpose and watch. This is the single most useful habit a new tester can build: deliberately introduce the bug your test is supposed to guard against, a wrong constant, a flipped comparison, a dropped condition, and run the test. If it still passes, it was never protecting anything; it was decoration.

Beyond that experiment, three questions separate real tests from green ones. Does the test's name state a behavior someone cares about, so a failure reads like a diagnosis? Would it fail for the right reason, meaning the assert compares against an expectation that came from the requirement, not from copying whatever the code currently outputs? And is it independent, passing alone, in the full suite, and on a fresh checkout, because it built its own world instead of inheriting leftovers?

A passing test proves the code did what the test expected today. A good test additionally proves it would scream if the behavior changed. The mutation experiment is how you check the second claim, and it takes thirty seconds.
What's the real difference between a unit test and an assert statement inside the production code? They both check conditions.

They check conditions for different audiences, at different times, against different sources of truth.

An assert inside production code guards an assumption the programmer believes can never be false: this list is never empty here, this value was validated at the border. It runs in production, forever, and if it fires it means the program itself is broken, an internal belief was wrong. Its expectation comes from the code's own logic.

A unit test verifies a promise made to someone else: members get 10% off, a full cart ships free. It runs in development and CI, not in the shipped program, and if it fires it means the behavior drifted from the specification. Its expectation comes from outside the code, from the requirement.

The practical consequences follow. Assertions should be cheap, always on, and reserved for 'this cannot happen' conditions, never for validating user input, which can happen and needs real handling. Tests should cover the behaviors users and callers rely on, including the awkward inputs, because those are promises, not assumptions.

Use both. Assertions document what the code believes; tests document what the code owes.
A senior dev reviewed my tax test and said 'this test can't fail'. What does that mean, and how do I check for it?

arguments.code:
RATE = 0.07  # the spec says the tax rate is 8%

def price_with_tax(price):
    return round(price * (1 + RATE), 2)

# Test 1: expectation derived from the code under test
expected_1 = round(100 * (1 + RATE), 2)
print(f"test 1 (mirror):  expected {expected_1}, got {price_with_tax(100)}",
      "->", "PASS" if price_with_tax(100) == expected_1 else "FAIL")

# Test 2: expectation taken from the spec, written as a literal
expected_2 = 108.00
print(f"test 2 (spec):    expected {expected_2}, got {price_with_tax(100)}",
      "->", "PASS" if price_with_tax(100) == expected_2 else "FAIL")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
test 1 (mirror):  expected 107.0, got 107.0 -> PASS
test 2 (spec):    expected 108.0, got 107.0 -> FAIL

'This test can't fail' means the test derives its expectation from the very code it is checking, so it is a mirror, not a measurement. Test 1 above computes its expected value with the same RATE constant the function uses. The rate is wrong, the spec says 8%, the code says 7%, and the test is green, because both sides of the comparison are wrong in exactly the same way. That test would pass with RATE set to anything at all.

Test 2 writes the expectation as a literal taken from the spec: a $100 item at 8% costs $108.00. It fails, correctly, and now the failure points at the real defect.

The audit is simple: for each test, ask where the expected value came from. If the answer is 'I ran the code and used what it printed' or 'I reused the code's own constants and helpers', the test can only catch typos, never wrong behavior. Expectations should enter the test from the requirement, a hand-worked example, or an independent calculation, never from the implementation.
How many assertions should one test have? My lead keeps saying 'one assert per test', but that seems extreme.

Your lead's rule is a compressed version of a better rule: one behavior per test. Assertions are cheap; behaviors are the unit that matters.

A single behavior often needs several asserts to describe it completely. 'Placing an order' might legitimately assert that an order id was assigned, that the status is pending, and that the total matches the cart, because those three facts are one behavior, and if any of them is wrong the same thing is broken. Splitting them into three tests adds ceremony without adding information.

What the one-assert slogan is really policing is the test that wanders: it creates an order, then checks the confirmation email, then verifies the inventory decrement, then tests a discount rule. When that test fails, four unrelated suspects line up, and the assert that fired hides the state of the other three because execution stopped.

So count behaviors, not asserts. If you can name the test with one sentence about one behavior, the number of asserts inside is your business. If the name needs an 'and', split the test.
We're building a parking-fee calculator from a written spec and the code doesn't exist yet. Can tests really come first here, or is that a slogan?

arguments.code:
# Spec: $4 for the first hour or part of one, $2 per additional hour
# or part, daily cap $20, lost ticket is a flat $25.

import math

def fee(hours, lost=False):
    if lost:
        return 25
    whole = math.ceil(hours)
    return 4 + 2 * (whole - 1)   # note: no daily cap yet

CASES = [
    ("first hour or part: 30 min",   fee(0.5),        4),
    ("exactly one hour",             fee(1),          4),
    ("part of hour two rounds up",   fee(1.2),        6),
    ("five hours",                   fee(5),         12),
    ("daily cap: twelve hours",      fee(12),        20),
    ("lost ticket flat rate",        fee(3, lost=True), 25),
]
for name, got, expected in CASES:
    print(f"{'PASS' if got == expected else 'FAIL'}  {name}: expected {expected}, got {got}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
PASS  first hour or part: 30 min: expected 4, got 4
PASS  exactly one hour: expected 4, got 4
PASS  part of hour two rounds up: expected 6, got 6
PASS  five hours: expected 12, got 12
FAIL  daily cap: twelve hours: expected 20, got 26
PASS  lost ticket flat rate: expected 25, got 25

This is the one situation where test-first is not a slogan but the natural order of work, because the spec already contains everything a test needs: concrete clauses with concrete numbers. Each test above is one spec clause wearing a name. Five pass against a first implementation. One fails, 'daily cap: twelve hours', and its failure is precise: the clause exists in the spec, the implementation computes $26 because nobody wrote the cap yet, and the failing test is effectively the remaining work list.

Notice what the tests did not need: the implementation. The expectations came from the document, so the suite can be written, reviewed, and even argued over before any code exists, and disagreements about what the spec means surface as disagreements about tests, which are cheap to settle.

Writing code then becomes a focused job: make the spec's own examples pass, one red clause at a time, without inventing behavior the spec never promised.
What is an 'equivalence class' in testing? It sounds like math vocabulary for something simple.

It is something simple: an equivalence class is a group of inputs your code treats the same way, same branch, same rule, same kind of answer. If shipping is free at $75 and over and costs $8 below it, then $10, $40, and $74.99 are one class, they all take the paid-shipping path, and $75, $200, and $10,000 are another.

The testing consequence is the useful part. Testing ten inputs from one class teaches you barely more than testing one, because they all exercise the same code path. Testing one representative from every class teaches you about every rule the code has. So the craft is: read the requirement, list the classes it implies (each tier, each validity region, each special case), pick one representative per class, then add the edges where classes meet, because that's where the mistakes live.

When someone says 'we tested a hundred inputs', the equivalence-class question is: from how many classes? A hundred inputs from two classes is two tests wearing a crowd costume.
Our free-shipping rule is 'orders of $50 or more ship free'. A customer with exactly a $50 order got charged shipping, but my tests pass: I used $30 and $80. What went wrong with my tests?

arguments.code:
def shipping_buggy(total):
    return 0 if total > 50 else 8   # spec: free at $50 or more

CASES = [
    (30.00, 8),    # the tests that existed
    (80.00, 0),    # the tests that existed
    (49.99, 8),    # just below the boundary
    (50.00, 0),    # the boundary itself
    (50.01, 0),    # just above the boundary
]
for total, expected in CASES:
    got = shipping_buggy(total)
    mark = "PASS" if got == expected else "FAIL"
    print(f"{mark}  total {total:6.2f}: expected shipping {expected}, got {got}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
PASS  total  30.00: expected shipping 8, got 8
PASS  total  80.00: expected shipping 0, got 0
PASS  total  49.99: expected shipping 8, got 8
FAIL  total  50.00: expected shipping 0, got 8
PASS  total  50.01: expected shipping 0, got 0

Your two tests sampled the interior of each equivalence class, $30 from the paid class and $80 from the free class, and interiors are where code is almost always right. The bug lives exactly where the rule changes its mind, at $50 itself, where the code says `>` and the spec says 'or more'. No interior test can ever see that difference, because `>` and `>=` agree everywhere except at the boundary.

The repair to your testing habit, not just this test: for every threshold in a requirement, test the value just below, the value itself, and the value just above. Those three inputs are the cheapest bug-detection in all of testing, because off-by-one errors, the commonest defect species in software, can only hide at edges.

Note the customer's $50.00 order was not an exotic edge case. Boundaries are where real users constantly land: exactly at the free-shipping line, exactly at the discount threshold, exactly at the form's character limit.
I'm testing a ticket-pricing function with age tiers: under 12 is child, 12 to 17 is teen, 18 to 64 is adult, 65 and over is senior. Which ages should I actually test?

arguments.code:
def band(age):
    if age < 12: return "child"
    if age < 18: return "teen"
    if age < 65: return "adult"
    return "senior"

# last and first member of every class, plus one interior per class
AGES = [0, 5, 11, 12, 15, 17, 18, 40, 64, 65, 90]
for age in AGES:
    print(f"age {age:3d} -> {band(age)}")

age   5 -> child
age  11 -> child
age  12 -> teen
age  15 -> teen
age  17 -> teen
age  18 -> adult
age  40 -> adult
age  64 -> adult
age  65 -> senior

Test the seam ages, not a scatter of birthdays. Every tier contributes two critical values: its last member and the first member of the next tier. That gives you 11 and 12 around the child/teen seam, 17 and 18 at teen/adult, 64 and 65 at adult/senior, plus the extremes 0 and a large age, and one interior per tier (5, 15, 40) as a sanity check that the class works at all.

Eleven ages sounds like a lot until you compare it with the information: a test at 15 and a test at 16 run the identical code path and can only disagree if the code is nondeterministic, while the pair 17/18 is the only place an off-by-one in the teen boundary can be caught. If the tiers were written with `<` where `<=` belonged, random age sampling might never land on the one wrong age.

General rule for any tiered rule: enumerate the tiers from the requirement, then spend your tests at the joints between them.
I tested my pricing function with 25 random ages and found no bugs. My coworker tested 7 hand-picked ages and found two bugs. How is that possible?

Because bugs are not distributed evenly across the input space, and random sampling pretends they are. Pricing rules change behavior at seams, the tier edges, the thresholds, the caps. A random age lands in a tier interior almost every time, and interiors are where the code is already right. Twenty-five random ages is roughly twenty-five repetitions of 'the middle of a tier still works'.

Your coworker's seven ages were not luckier; they were aimed. Hand-picked boundary values sit exactly where `>` gets confused with `>=`, where a tier starts one year early, where a cap is applied one step late. Two bugs at two seams is the normal yield.

There is a second, quieter problem with random test inputs: when one fails, you often can't tell which property it violated, and the failing case changes every run unless you record the seed. Random generation has a real place in testing, in property-style checks over thousands of cases with a recorded seed, but as a substitute for thinking about where the rules change, it's just rolling dice in the dark.

Test design beats test volume. Choose inputs the way the requirement is structured.
A username validator accepts 3 to 20 characters. In production it rejected a valid 20-character username. Show me how boundary testing would have caught this before it shipped.

arguments.code:
def valid_buggy(name):
    return 3 <= len(name) < 20   # spec: 3 to 20 characters, inclusive

CASES = [
    (2,  False),  # just under the minimum
    (3,  True),   # the minimum itself
    (4,  True),   # just over the minimum
    (19, True),   # just under the maximum
    (20, True),   # the maximum itself
    (21, False),  # just over the maximum
]
for length, expected in CASES:
    got = valid_buggy("x" * length)
    mark = "PASS" if got == expected else "FAIL"
    print(f"{mark}  length {length:2d}: expected valid={expected}, got {got}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
PASS  length  2: expected valid=False, got False
PASS  length  3: expected valid=True, got True
PASS  length  4: expected valid=True, got True
PASS  length 19: expected valid=True, got True
FAIL  length 20: expected valid=True, got False
PASS  length 21: expected valid=False, got False

For any range in a requirement, the boundary pattern is six values: just below the minimum, the minimum, just above it, just below the maximum, the maximum, and just above it. Run against the production bug, a `< 20` where `<= 20` belonged, five of the six pass and exactly one fails: length 20, the precise case your user hit.

This is the pattern's power. The defect is a single character in the source, and it is invisible to every input except one specific length. A test suite built from 'a short name, a normal name, a long name' samples lengths like 5, 9, and 14, all deep in the interior, all green, while the one wrong length sails to production.

Ranges are everywhere once you look: string lengths, quantities, ages, prices, retry counts, page sizes. Every time a requirement says 'between A and B', the six-value pattern is the test, and it costs almost nothing to write.
Can you show me equivalence classes on something small, like converting a percentage score to a letter grade?

    if score >= 90: return "A"
    if score >= 80: return "B"
    if score >= 70: return "C"
    if score >= 60: return "D"
    return "F"

# one representative per class, plus the seam scores around each cut
CASES = [(95, "A"), (90, "A"), (89, "B"), (83, "B"), (80, "B"),
         (79, "C"), (65, "D"), (60, "D"), (59, "F"), (20, "F")]
for score, expected in CASES:
    got = grade(score)
    mark = "PASS" if got == expected else "FAIL"
    print(f"{mark}  score {score:3d}: expected {expected}, got {got}")

messages.content:
PASS  score  95: expected A, got A
PASS  score  90: expected A, got A
PASS  score  89: expected B, got B
PASS  score  83: expected B, got B
PASS  score  80: expected B, got B
PASS  score  79: expected C, got C
PASS  score  65: expected D, got D
PASS  score  60: expected D, got D

When you design cases for any classification rule, ask two questions in order: what are the classes, and where exactly does one stop and the next start? Answer those and the test list writes itself.
Why do experienced testers obsess over boundaries instead of just testing lots of normal, realistic inputs?

Because of where code physically changes its mind. Inside a range, a function executes one fixed path; nothing about the input's exact value alters which lines run. At a boundary, a comparison flips, a tier changes, a cap engages, a loop runs one more or one fewer time. Every one of those flips is a place a programmer can be wrong by one, and being wrong by one is the single most common defect pattern in software.

Normal inputs have a second weakness: they mostly confirm each other. The fiftieth realistic order total exercises the same path as the previous forty-nine. Testers aren't bored by normal inputs because they're snobs; they're rationing effort. A suite of twenty aimed inputs, class representatives plus every seam, routinely finds bugs that two hundred realistic inputs walk straight past.

Realistic inputs still earn their place as a final sanity layer, a few end-to-end cases proving the system works on data shaped like production. But they are the garnish. The meal is classes and boundaries, because that's the geography where bugs actually live.
My discount function is supposed to clamp percentages into the range 0 to 100. What does a proper partition test for that look like?

def clamp_buggy(pct):
    if pct > 100:
        return 100
    return pct   # forgot the lower clamp

CASES = [
    (-5,  0),    # below the range: invalid region
    (0,   0),    # the lower boundary itself
    (25,  25),   # interior
    (100, 100),  # the upper boundary itself
    (140, 100),  # above the range: invalid region
]
for pct, expected in CASES:
    got = clamp_buggy(pct)
    mark = "PASS" if got == expected else "FAIL"
    print(f"{mark}  clamp({pct:4d}): expected {expected}, got {got}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
FAIL  clamp(  -5): expected 0, got -5
PASS  clamp(   0): expected 0, got 0
PASS  clamp(  25): expected 25, got 25
PASS  clamp( 100): expected 100, got 100
PASS  clamp( 140): expected 100, got 100

Partition testing means one case per region the rule defines, and crucially, the invalid regions are regions too. This clamp has five: below zero, exactly zero, the interior, exactly one hundred, and above one hundred. Four of the five pass against the buggy version. The below-range case fails, because the implementation only ever clamps the top; a -5% discount flows through and quietly becomes a 5% surcharge downstream.

The mistake this catches is a mindset, not a typo: developers test the inputs they expect users to send. But clamping exists precisely for inputs nobody expected, so a partition suite that omits the invalid regions tests the clamp everywhere except where it earns its keep.

Whenever a requirement describes a range, write the regions down first, valid and invalid alike, then give each region one representative and each border a direct hit. The list is short, and it is complete in a way 'a bunch of percentages' never is.
Leap years: divisible by 4, except century years, unless divisible by 400. How do testers turn a nested rule like that into a test set?

arguments.code:
def is_leap(year):
    return year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)

def is_leap_naive(year):   # the version that only remembers the first clause
    return year % 4 == 0

CASES = [
    (2023, False, "plain year: not divisible by 4"),
    (2024, True,  "divisible by 4: the base clause"),
    (1900, False, "century year: the exception"),
    (2000, True,  "divisible by 400: the exception to the exception"),
    (2100, False, "next century year: exception again"),
]
for year, expected, clause in CASES:
    got = is_leap(year)
    mark = "PASS" if got == expected else "FAIL"
    naive = is_leap_naive(year)
    note = "" if naive == expected else f"  (naive %4 rule says {naive})"
    print(f"{mark}  {year}: expected {expected}, got {got}  <- {clause}{note}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
PASS  2023: expected False, got False  <- plain year: not divisible by 4
PASS  2024: expected True, got True  <- divisible by 4: the base clause
PASS  1900: expected False, got False  <- century year: the exception  (naive %4 rule says True)
PASS  2000: expected True, got True  <- divisible by 400: the exception to the exception
PASS  2100: expected False, got False  <- next century year: exception again  (naive %4 rule says True)

A nested rule like this is a gift to the tester, because its clauses are the equivalence classes, spelled out by the rule itself. One case per clause: an ordinary year for the base divisibility test, a plain divisible-by-4 year where the base clause fires, a century year where the exception overrides it, and a divisible-by-400 year where the exception to the exception overrides that. Four clauses, four cases, plus one extra century year for confidence.

The comparison column shows the yield. The naive rule that only implements 'divisible by 4' passes the two easy cases and fails exactly at 1900 and 2100, the exception years, which is where every hand-rolled leap-year function in production is wrong. Random year testing would need luck to land on a century year at all; clause-driven testing starts there.

Generalize the move: whenever a requirement contains 'except', 'unless', or 'but only if', each of those words marks a class, and each class deserves its own named test.
Boundaries make sense for numbers. What are the equivalent test cases for a text field, like a display name?

For text, the classes are defined by how the code handles the string, not by its content. Walk the handling rules and each one spawns cases. Length: the empty string, a single character, exactly the maximum, one over the maximum. Whitespace: spaces only, leading and trailing spaces (does the code trim, and does the test agree with the product decision?), tabs and newlines inside the value. Character classes: accented letters, an emoji, a combining character, right-to-left text, a name longer in bytes than in characters, which is where naive length checks and databases disagree. Hostile shapes: quotes and angle brackets that will later meet SQL or HTML, and the string that looks like a number.

Two more that catch real bugs: a missing value versus an empty value, which many systems treat differently while users treat them as identical, and a duplicate of an existing name with different capitalization or spacing.

The method is the same as for numbers. Don't brainstorm random names; enumerate the decisions the code makes about strings, then write one input per decision point and one at each length seam.
What is a test fixture? Every test in my file starts with the same six lines of setup copied and pasted.

A fixture is the world a test needs to exist before its behavior can happen: the objects created, the data loaded, the state arranged. Your six copied lines are a fixture that hasn't been factored out yet.

The copies are a problem for two reasons beyond tidiness. When the setup needs to change, and it will, because constructors and required fields evolve, you must edit it in forty places, and you will miss one, producing a test that fails for setup reasons and sends you debugging the wrong thing. And the repetition buries each test's actual point: the reader can't tell which of the six lines this particular test cares about and which are ceremony.

The fix is to extract the shared world-building into one named place, a setup function, a fixture provided by the framework, or a factory that builds the object, so each test reads as: given this world (named, shared), when this happens, then this holds. The individual test then only mentions the setup details that are special about it, which is exactly the information a reader needs.

One caution that the rest of fixture craft is about: extract the building, but never share the built thing between tests if tests can mutate it. Shared construction, fresh instances.
My cart tests pass when I run them one at a time but fail when I run the whole file. What is usually behind that?

This is the polluted fixture, the commonest cause of 'passes alone, fails in the suite'. Both tests share one cart object built once at module level. Run alone, test_add_two starts with an empty cart and passes. Run after test_add_one, it inherits the pen the earlier test left behind, counts three items, and fails, even though the code under test is perfectly correct.

The deep problem isn't this failure; it's that every test's verdict now depends on execution order and on what its neighbors did, which destroys the one thing a suite is for: a failure meaning 'this behavior is broken'.

The fix is the fixture rule: share the recipe, never the dish. Each test builds its own cart (here, two lines; in real suites, a setup function or factory called per test). Setup gets slightly more expensive and completely boring, which is the correct trade. State that a test did not create is state that can betray it.

This is the factory pattern, and it fixes the readability problem by inverting the defaults. A fixture describes a whole object once and forces every test to inherit all of it. A factory gives every field a sensible default and lets each test override only the fields its behavior is about, so the test's setup line becomes a precise statement of what matters: `make_user(role='admin', active=False)` says 'this test is about an inactive admin' and nothing else needs reading.

The nine required fields still get filled, by the defaults, so the object is always valid. But the test no longer breaks when an irrelevant field is added to the model, and a reader never has to diff a nine-line setup against the last test's nine-line setup to find the one meaningful difference.

Rule of thumb: fixtures suit a fixed world several tests share read-only; factories suit objects whose relevant property changes from test to test. Most growing suites end up factory-first.
Building a fresh database for every test makes my suite take ten minutes. Sharing one database makes tests interfere. Is there a middle way?

Yes, and finding it starts with separating two costs you're currently paying as one. Isolation failures come from shared mutable state. Slowness comes from expensive construction. They have different solutions.

The usual middle way has three layers. Build the expensive, immutable scaffolding once per suite or module: schema, migrations, reference data like country lists and tax tables that no test ever modifies. Give each test cheap isolation on top of it: wrap the test in a transaction and roll it back, or truncate only the tables tests write to, or hand each test its own schema or tenant id in a shared database. Then reserve true fresh-database construction for the handful of tests that genuinely test database-level behavior like migrations.

The principle to hold onto: isolation must be per test, but construction doesn't have to be. Rollback gives you a world that looks freshly built, because every change the test made is undone, at a fraction of the cost of building it.

And profile before optimizing. Often three tests are doing full imports or seed loads they don't need, and fixing those beats restructuring the whole suite.

Some of my tests have 30 lines of setup and 2 lines of actual test. Is that just how it is for complex domains?

Sometimes, but usually a 30-to-2 ratio is a design signal, not a domain tax. Setup that long means the test is building its world at too low a level: constructing objects field by field, wiring collaborators by hand, replaying five business steps to reach the state it needs. Each of those is work the system itself already knows how to do.

Three compressions usually collapse it. Build through the public API: instead of hand-crafting an order row with eleven fields, call the place-order function with a small cart, so setup becomes two lines and doubles as a smoke test of order creation. Extract a factory or builder with defaults for the objects that recur, so each test states only what's special. And name the recurring worlds: a helper called `given_a_paid_order()` hides a whole saga behind the one fact the test cares about.

What's left after compression should read like the 'given' clause of the behavior: given a paid order and a closed store, when the refund runs, then it is queued. If setup still runs long after that, the honest conclusion is different: the behavior itself is hard to reach, which means the code's seams are in the wrong places, and the test is reporting a design problem.
I was told never to share fixtures between tests, but my price table fixture is shared by forty tests and nothing has ever gone wrong. Was the advice wrong?

The advice was compressed, and your price table is the case the compression hides. The real rule is not 'never share'; it's 'never share anything a test can mutate'. Sharing is dangerous because of state that changes, leftovers from one test leaking into the next. A price table that every test only reads cannot leak, because reading leaves the world exactly as it was. Forty tests sharing a read-only table are forty tests sharing a constant, and constants are safe.

The trap is that 'read-only' is a discipline, not a property, unless you enforce it. The day one test adjusts a price 'just for this case' by writing into the shared table, it silently rewrites the world for the other thirty-nine, and the failures that follow will blame innocent tests. So if you share, make the sharing honest: build the table once, and where the language allows, freeze it, or have the factory hand each test a copy when it needs to modify prices, keeping the shared original pristine.

Shared construction with fresh or immutable instances is the goal. Your forty tests are fine. Just make sure test forty-one can't edit the table.
Fixture, factory, builder: I see all three in our codebase and they seem to do the same job. When do I actually reach for each?

They solve the same problem, getting a valid object into a test, at different points on the spectrum of 'how much varies between tests'.

A fixture is a fixed, pre-built world: this exact store, these exact three products, this customer with an order history. Reach for it when many tests genuinely share one world and mostly read from it, like integration tests against a seeded scenario. Its weakness is rigidity: the test that needs one thing different must fork the whole world.

A factory is a function that builds a fresh, valid object with sensible defaults, letting the test override what it cares about: `make_user(role='admin')`. Reach for it when the same kind of object appears everywhere but each test stresses a different property. This is the workhorse of most suites.

A builder is a fluent, step-by-step assembler, `OrderBuilder().with_item(x).with_discount().paid().build()`, for objects whose construction has meaningful stages or many interacting options, where the sequence of steps is itself part of what varies. Reach for it when factories grow a dozen keyword arguments that only make sense in combination.

If you're unsure, start with a factory. It's the simplest one that keeps tests independent, and most codebases need builders in exactly two or three places, not everywhere.
To test refunds I hand-build order rows in the exact database shape, with eleven fields. A colleague says I should create the orders through the real checkout code instead. Why would that be better?

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
Your colleague is right, for a reason that compounds over time. A hand-built row encodes your current belief about what an order looks like: eleven fields, in today's shape, with today's invariants. The moment checkout changes how totals are computed, adds a field, or tightens an invariant, your hand-built orders become fossils, objects the real system could never produce. Your refund tests then verify refunds against orders that cannot exist, and they can pass while refunds against real orders break.

Building through the public API inverts that. The setup can only create states the system itself can reach, so the test is honest by construction. It also means your setup doubles as a smoke test: if order creation breaks, the refund tests fail at setup and tell you so, instead of testing refunds in a fantasy world.

The cost is real, setup runs more code and can be slower, and occasionally you need a state the API can't easily reach, which is a legitimate reason to drop to hand-building for that case. But the default should be: enter through the front door, because tests should live in the same world as production.
There's a test in our suite everyone calls 'the mystery guest': it passes in the full suite but fails when run alone, and nobody knows why. What is it telling us?

It's telling you the test has an undeclared dependency: it uses something it does not create. Run alone, that something doesn't exist, so it fails. Run in the suite, some earlier test creates it as a side effect, a row, a file, a cache entry, a configured setting, and the mystery guest quietly helps itself. The test isn't testing your code; it's testing the residue of its neighbors.

This is worse than a merely flaky test, because its green checkmark in CI is evidence about execution order, not about behavior. Reorder the suite, parallelize it, or delete the unrelated test that feeds it, and it collapses, usually at the worst moment.

The hunt is mechanical: run the test alone to confirm the failure, then binary-search the suite, running it after halves of the other tests, until you find the smallest set that makes it pass. That set contains its secret benefactor. Then read the test for everything it touches that it didn't build: shared seed data, module-level state, files, singletons.

The fix is always the same shape: the test must declare and create everything it needs, even if that makes it longer. A test that brings its own world can run first, last, alone, or in parallel, and its verdict means the same thing in all four worlds.
What is mocking, actually? I nod along in meetings but I've never done it.

Mocking is replacing a real collaborator with a stand-in you control, for the duration of one test. Your code calls the payment gateway, the clock, the email service, the network. In a test, those real things are slow, expensive, outside your control, or capable of sending real email to real people, so you swap in a double: an object with the same interface that behaves the way the test dictates and often records how it was used.

The point is isolation with control. Testing whether your checkout handles a declined card should not require a real card that declines. You instruct the double to decline, run the checkout, and assert your code responded correctly. You have tested your behavior under a condition the real world would make painful to arrange.

Two disciplines separate useful mocking from self-deception, and they're worth learning with the technique itself. Mock at the boundaries of your system, the external services and clocks, not your own internal classes, or you'll spend your life updating tests that merely mirror your code. And make the double's behavior come from reality, recorded responses, documented shapes, because a double that behaves the way you imagine the service behaves tests your imagination.

Start small: the clock and one external API cover most real needs.
Our user-greeting test has been green for months, but production throws a KeyError on the same code path. The test mocks the user API. How can both be true?

test:       Hello, Ada Lovelace -> PASS
production: KeyError 'full_name' -> the green test never saw the real shape

Both are true because the test never met the real API. The double was written from the author's imagination of the response shape, and the code was then written (or drifted) to match the double. The test verifies that the code and the mock agree with each other, which they do, perfectly, in a closed loop that excludes reality. Production uses the real key, 'name', the code asks for 'full_name', and the loop is broken by a KeyError the suite structurally cannot produce.

This is the central hazard of mocking: a mock encodes an assumption, and an unverified assumption in a test is a lie with a green checkmark. The defenses are boring and effective. Build doubles from captured reality: record real API responses and replay those as your fake payloads. Prefer fakes that implement the documented contract over mocks that return whatever the test wants. And keep at least a thin layer of contract or integration tests that talk to the real service, or a sandbox of it, whose entire job is to detect the day the real shape and your assumption part ways.

Mock the boundary, yes. But let reality author the mock's lines.

The difference is where the seam goes. Mocking datetime means reaching into the standard library from the test and patching the concept of 'now' for the whole process: fragile, global, and it breaks the day the implementation calls time through a different import path. Injection means the function stops helping itself to the current time and instead receives 'today' as an ordinary parameter, as this version does. In production, the caller passes the real date. In the test, you pass any date you like, including the exact boundary days, as plain data.

Look at what the test becomes: no patching machinery, no framework magic, just three calls with three dates, including day 14, the boundary, which is precisely the case time-dependent bugs live in and precisely the case you could never reliably arrange by waiting or by patching.

The design lesson generalizes: a function that reaches out for the clock, the network, or randomness is a function with hidden inputs. Making those inputs explicit parameters is a small refactor that converts untestable code into trivially testable code, and usually makes the production code clearer too.
Half my tests mock our own internal classes, and every refactor breaks twenty tests even when behavior is unchanged. Is that normal?

It's common, and it's the signature of mocking at the wrong level. When you mock your own internals, the test stops describing behavior and starts describing wiring: this class must call that helper with these arguments in this order. The test has memorized the implementation. Any refactor, which by definition changes the wiring while keeping the behavior, breaks the memorization, and twenty tests fail to announce that nothing is actually wrong.

The damage compounds. A suite that cries wolf on every refactor trains the team to update tests mechanically until they're green again, which quietly deletes their protective value, and eventually trains them to fear refactoring altogether.

The correction is to move the mocking boundary outward. Test your internal classes through their public behavior, with real instances of each other, because your own code is fast, deterministic, and under your control; it doesn't need doubles. Reserve mocks for what crosses the system's edge: external APIs, the clock, the filesystem, email, payment providers, the things that are slow, unreliable, or not yours.

A useful test of a test: if I rewrote the internals completely and the behavior stayed identical, would this test still pass? For behavior tests the answer is yes. For wiring tests it's no, and those are the ones to rewrite or delete.
Should I assert that my code called the email mock with the right arguments, or assert something else? The call-assertions feel brittle.

Your instinct is right, and the distinction has a name: interaction verification versus state verification. Asserting the mock was called with exact arguments verifies an interaction, one specific way of achieving the outcome. Asserting that an email with the right recipient and subject exists in a fake outbox verifies the outcome itself.

Interaction assertions are brittle for a structural reason: there are usually several correct ways to produce the same outcome. Batch the sends, change the call order, add a parameter, route through a queue, and the outcome is unchanged while every interaction assertion breaks. You've coupled the test to the choreography instead of the result.

State verification survives all of that, because it checks what the user of the system would check: did the email arrive, with the right content, once.

Interactions do have one legitimate home: when the call itself is the outcome. Charging a card exactly once, not twice, is an interaction fact with no resulting state you can easily inspect, and there a call count is the honest assertion. The rule: verify state when state exists; verify interactions only when the interaction is the deliverable.

The simplest honest double for a sender is a recording stub: same send interface, no network, and an outbox list where every message lands for inspection. If checkout is later refactored to build the message differently or send through a helper, the test still passes, because what it protects is the outcome a customer experiences.

When is mocking actually legitimate? Testing purists at work act like any mock is a smell.

Mocking is legitimate exactly where the real thing makes the test worse in a way that has nothing to do with your code's correctness. There are five classic cases. The collaborator is slow: a real API call turns a millisecond test into a two-second one, multiplied by a thousand tests. It's external and uncontrolled: the payment provider's sandbox is down, or rate-limited, or changes without asking you. It's nondeterministic: the clock, randomness, the network. It has side effects you cannot allow in a test: sending real email, charging real cards, deleting real files. Or it doesn't exist yet: you're building against an API another team ships next month.

Notice the pattern: in every case you're replacing something at the edge of your system, something that is not the thing you're testing. The purists' real grievance isn't with doubles; it's with mocking your own internals until the tests describe your wiring diagram instead of your behavior, and with doubles whose behavior was invented rather than observed.

So the working rule: mock at the boundary, faithfully, and test your own code for real. A suite that follows it gets the speed and control without the self-deception.
Our payment mock returns a response shape from two years ago. The real API changed its shape last spring and nobody noticed until a production bug. How do teams prevent mock drift like that?

Drift is the default outcome for any double whose behavior is maintained by memory, so teams prevent it by removing memory from the loop. Three mechanisms, in increasing strength.

First, source the double from captured reality. Record actual responses from the real API (sanitized) and build your fakes and stubs from those recordings. When the API changes, re-recording is a deliberate act that produces a visible diff, instead of a silent divergence.

Second, write contract tests: a small, separate suite whose only job is to run the same expectations against both the double and the real service (or its sandbox). The day the real shape changes, the contract test against the real service fails while the one against the double passes, and the gap is the drift, named and dated, in CI rather than in production.

Third, keep the mocked surface small. Every field your code reads from a response is a field that can drift; code that depends on three fields of a forty-field response has a three-field drift surface. Read narrowly, and put the reading in one adapter module so the contract tests have exactly one place to stand.

The mindset underneath all three: a double is a claim about another system, and claims about other systems need re-verification on a schedule, because the other system is not standing still.
A testing book says 'don't mock what you don't own'. But I have to test code that calls a third-party API. What am I supposed to do?

The slogan isn't 'never fake the third-party API'. It's about where the fake lives. If your tests mock the third-party library's classes directly, your tests become coupled to that library's interface: its method names, its exception types, its pagination quirks. When the library upgrades, your tests break everywhere, and worse, your production code tends to grow shaped like the library too.

The standard move is to wrap the third-party API in a thin adapter that you do own: your code talks to `BillingGateway.charge(customer, amount)` in your vocabulary, and the adapter translates to the vendor's SDK. Then the rule resolves itself. In your tests, you mock your adapter, which you own, with behavior in your terms. The adapter itself gets a small number of integration or contract tests against the real vendor sandbox, because it's the one place where vendor reality must be faced.

This buys you three things: tests that survive vendor upgrades, production code that speaks your domain's language, and a single seam to cut if you ever switch providers. The adapter is not bureaucracy; it's the border checkpoint where an external system's chaos gets translated into your system's calm.

Something odd happened on my team: new hires implement features to match the mocks in the tests, but production behaves differently from the mocks, and now nobody is sure which one is 'correct'. How does a suite rot like this?

It rots through a quiet inversion of authority. Mocks are supposed to be downstream of reality: the real service behaves somehow, and the double imitates it. But doubles are easier to read than the real system's documentation, they're right there in the repo, and they're always available. New hires quite reasonably treat the tests as the specification of the outside world. When implementation and mock disagree, they 'fix' the implementation, because the test is the thing that must go green. Each such fix moves the code toward the mock and away from production, and nobody notices, because the suite is green and the divergence only manifests against the real service, which the suite no longer touches.

The root cause is almost always an old unverified assumption: a mock written from imagination, never checked against the real API, slowly promoted by familiarity into the team's source of truth.

Recovery has a specific order. First, establish ground truth from the real system: its documentation, its sandbox, recorded live responses. Second, fix the doubles to match reality, and expect a wave of red tests; those failures are the map of everywhere the code absorbed the fiction. Third, fix the code where the code was wrong, and delete code that only existed to satisfy a fiction. Finally, install the guard that prevents recurrence: contract tests against the real service, so the double's authority is borrowed and periodically re-verified, never owned.

The lesson to keep: a mock is a rumor about another system. Useful, often necessary, but a rumor, and rumors should never outrank the source.
I don't want to replace my pricing function with a mock, but I do want to verify the bulk-order path actually uses it per line item. Is there something between a mock and nothing?

Yes: a spy. A mock replaces the function and returns invented values. A spy wraps the real function, records how it was used, and delegates, so the values flowing through your test are produced by the genuine pricing logic while you still get to inspect the interaction.

That's exactly the right tool for your question, because your question has two halves with different natures. 'What total does the bulk path produce?' is a behavior question, answered honestly only by the real pricing code. 'Does it price per line item, or once on the sum?' is a structural question about how the bulk path uses its collaborator, and the spy's call log answers it: three calls, one per item, each carrying the member flag.

Spies keep the fidelity of real code with the observability of a mock, at the price of running the real collaborator, so they suit collaborators that are fast, pure, and yours. The pattern to remember: mock what you must replace, spy on what you want to watch, and leave everything else real.
We have a few flaky tests that fail randomly maybe one run in twenty. The team just re-runs CI until it's green. Why do people say flaky tests are worse than no tests?

Because a test suite is an alarm system, and flakiness teaches everyone to ignore the alarm. The first cost is direct: a one-in-twenty failure means most red builds are noise, so the team re-runs reflexively, and the day a red build is a real regression, it gets re-run too, and merged. The signal is destroyed precisely by being usually meaningless.

The second cost is subtler: flaky tests make real intermittent bugs invisible. Some fraction of 'flaky tests' are not test defects at all; they're the suite detecting a genuine race, ordering assumption, or time dependence in the product, once in twenty runs. Re-running until green files those detections under 'test problem' and ships the bug.

A missing test, by contrast, is an honest gap. Nobody trusts it, nobody is confused by it, and it doesn't train the team to override red builds.

So the discipline is: a flaky test is a bug, in the test or in the code, and it gets fixed or quarantined with an owner and a ticket, never absorbed by retries. A suite the team believes is worth more than a bigger suite it doesn't.

You test randomness in two layers, because two different claims are being made. The first claim is about your sampling logic: given this source of randomness, does the function pick the right number of items, without repeats, from the right pool? That claim becomes fully testable the moment the randomness is seeded, or better, injected: pass the generator in, seed it with 42, and the 'random' draw is the same on every run, so you can assert its exact contents.

The second claim is about the randomness itself, that it's fair, unbiased, truly random. That is almost never your code's promise; it's the standard library's, and you don't test other people's promises. What you can assert unseeded are properties that hold for every draw: the size is right, there are no duplicates, everything came from the catalog. Those property assertions run against any seed.

The design move underneath is the same one as with clocks: randomness that a function helps itself to is a hidden input. Inject it, and the function becomes deterministic under test while staying random in production.

A test in our suite fails only when the whole suite runs, never alone, and the failure moves around depending on which tests we include. Where do I even start?

Start from what the symptom is proving: some test's verdict depends on state it didn't create, or it leaves state that changes a neighbor. Order dependence is never a mystery about the failing test alone; it's a relationship between tests, so hunt the relationship.

The standard technique is bisection over the suite. Run the failing test alone (passes). Run it with the first half of the suite before it; if it fails, the polluter is in that half; if it passes, add the second half. Halve until you find the smallest set of predecessors that makes it fail, then shrink to the single test whose presence flips the verdict. That test and yours share something: a global variable, a singleton, a file, a database table, a cache, an environment variable, a mock that wasn't torn down.

The usual suspects, in order of frequency: module-level mutable state mutated by a test, fixtures built once and written to, real files in a shared directory, database rows that leak between tests, and time or randomness that one test froze and forgot to release.

Once found, the fix is in the polluter or in the shared resource's isolation, not in the victim. And add a guard: run the suite in a shuffled order in CI, so the next coupling announces itself immediately instead of accumulating silently.

Besides obvious things like random numbers, what are the hidden sources of nondeterminism that make tests flaky?

The repeat offenders, roughly in order of how often they bite. Time: not just 'now', but time zones, daylight-saving transitions, and tests that pass except near midnight or month-end when a date rolls over. Ordering: iterating a set or an unordered query result and asserting on the sequence; hash randomization means string sets can iterate differently between processes, so the test passes on your machine and fails in CI. Concurrency: two operations racing, where the test asserts the state between them. External state: leftover files, database rows, caches warmed by a previous run. Environment: locale changing number and date formats, environment variables present in CI and absent locally, available memory changing timing. And network-shaped things even in 'unit' tests: DNS, a shared dev service someone else deploys to mid-run.

The hunting method is to make the invisible visible: when a test flakes, log the seed, the order, the timestamp, and the environment with the failure, then run the test in a loop, hundreds of times, and in shuffled suite order, until it fails for you locally. A flake you can reproduce on demand is already half fixed.

The design defense is the theme of this whole area: hidden inputs are the enemy. Time, randomness, ordering, and environment should enter functions as explicit, controllable inputs wherever a test needs to stand on them.
Half my date logic is basically untestable because it calls 'today' internally in five places. Is the answer really to refactor all of it?

Yes, but probably less of it than you fear, because the refactor has a natural stopping point: the boundary of each workflow. You don't need every helper to take a date parameter. You need the entry points, the functions that start a business operation, to accept 'now' (or a clock object) and pass it down to the helpers they call. Five call sites that read the clock usually collapse into one or two entry points that receive it.

The pattern that keeps it painless: give the parameter a production default at the outermost layer only, or have the top-level caller pass `date.today()` explicitly. Everything below that line treats time as ordinary data, which is what it is.

What you get back is larger than testability. Date logic fails at seams: month ends, leap days, DST, the instant a trial flips to expired. Those seams are unreachable when the clock is ambient, because you cannot arrange for today to be February 29th. Once time is an input, your test table can stand on every seam in the calendar in a millisecond each.

Teams resist this refactor because the code 'works'. But code whose correctness cannot be checked at its known danger points isn't working; it's unverified in exactly the places it is most likely to be wrong.

Management's solution to our flaky test problem is an auto-retry: CI re-runs failed tests up to three times and only reports failure if all three fail. As the person who maintains the suite, how should I think about this?

As a painkiller that also masks the disease, and the masking is the dangerous part. Auto-retry converts a one-in-twenty flake into a one-in-eight-thousand reported failure, which sounds like reliability and is actually blindness. Three things get hidden. Genuine intermittent product bugs, races and ordering faults that manifest rarely, now pass silently nearly every time; you have built a machine for shipping them. The suite's runtime and cost grow in proportion to its sickness, invisibly. And the data disappears: with retries, nobody can even say which tests flake or how often, because the flakiness leaves no trace in the results anyone reads.

If retries are imposed, negotiate the instrumentation that keeps them honest: retries allowed, but every retry is logged, counted, and reported as a flaky event with the test's name, and a dashboard shows the flake rate per test per week. A rising flake rate then triggers real work, and the worst offenders get quarantined, removed from the gating suite into a separate job with an owner and a fix-or-delete deadline.

Your position to argue is simple: a flaky test is a bug report, about the test or about the product, and retry-until-green is a policy of shredding bug reports. Stabilize the suite until retries are unnecessary, and treat any month where the flake count rises as a month the suite got worse, even if every build is green.

People talk about 'property-based testing' but my team just writes example tests. What's the actual idea, without buying into a whole framework?

Example tests check specific cases you thought of: this input gives that output. Property tests check a claim that should hold for all inputs: sorting never changes which elements exist, encoding then decoding returns the original, the total is never negative. You state the invariant once, then run the function against many generated inputs, ordinary, random, and deliberately hostile, and the machinery looks for a counterexample.

The shift is in where your thinking goes. With examples, you enumerate cases and your test quality is bounded by your imagination on the day you wrote them. With properties, you ask a harder and more valuable question: what is always true about this function's behavior, no matter what it's fed? Answering that question is design work; it frequently reveals that nobody had ever stated the function's real contract.

You don't need a framework to start. A loop that generates a few hundred varied inputs, seeded so failures reproduce, and asserts the invariant, captures most of the value. Frameworks add smarter generation and automatic shrinking of failing cases, which you can adopt later.

Use both: examples document the important specific cases in human terms; properties patrol the vast space between them.

Nobody had to predict the semicolon bug as a specific case in advance; they only had to generate values with hostile contents, separators, backslashes, empties, equals signs, and let the invariant 'what goes in must come back' judge them all. Example tests check the cases the author imagined. The round-trip checks the contract itself, and the contract is where serializer bugs live.

Every pair of inverse operations in your system is a round-trip property waiting to be written: save/load, serialize/parse, export/import, compress/decompress, encrypt/decrypt. They are the highest-yield properties in most codebases.

Property testing sounds great when you can state the expected output. But for half my functions I can't compute the right answer independently, that's why I wrote the function. What properties can I even state?

You're describing the normal case, and it's exactly what metamorphic properties are for: when you can't judge one output in isolation, judge the relationship between outputs.

The patterns recur across domains. Monotonicity: increasing the input should never decrease this output, as with tax owed versus income. Round-trips: encode then decode, save then load, returns the original. Idempotence: applying it twice equals applying it once, as with sorting, normalizing, or marking a job complete. Invariance under permutation: shuffling the input shouldn't change a sum, a count, a maximum, a set of results. Conservation: totals are preserved, money out plus money remaining equals money in. Bounds: the output always lies in a legal range, a percentage between 0 and 100, a count never negative. Agreement with a slow oracle: your optimized function and the naive, obviously-correct version may differ in speed but never in result, so generate inputs and compare the two.

That last one is often the unlock: most production functions have a dumb, trustworthy sibling, a brute-force search, a reference implementation, last year's version, that can serve as the expected-output machine for generated inputs.

Start by asking of any function: what would make me say 'that's obviously wrong' without knowing the right answer? Every answer to that question is a property.

If property tests check everything, why keep example tests at all? And if examples are clearer, why add properties? I need the honest division of labor.

They fail in opposite directions, which is why serious suites carry both.

Example tests are precise and legible. Each one documents a specific, humanly meaningful case: the member with a coupon on a Tuesday, the leap-day renewal, the order that exactly hits the free-shipping line. A new hire can read them as a specification, and when one fails, the case itself explains what broke. Their weakness is coverage of imagination: they patrol only the ground the author thought to stand on, and bugs breed in the unthought.

Property tests are broad and terse. One invariant plus generated inputs patrols thousands of cases, including the degenerate ones humans skip: empty, singleton, all-duplicates, maximum size, values with separators in them. Their weakness is legibility and aim: a property failure arrives as a strange counterexample that needs shrinking and interpretation, and a property can only guard what can be stated as an invariant; 'the confirmation email should sound friendly' has no property form.

The working division: examples pin the cases that matter to the business and document intent; properties defend the contract's shape across the input space. And the two feed each other. Every counterexample a property finds, once shrunk, becomes a permanent example, so the suite's memory of every wound is kept in the most readable form.

Fake, mock, stub, dummy, spy: five words that all seem to mean 'not the real thing'. What is each one actually for?

They're all test doubles, but each has a different job, and using the right name helps you pick the right tool.

A dummy is a placeholder that fills a required parameter and is never used: the address object you must pass but the code path never touches. A stub returns canned answers: ask it anything, it hands back the response the test scripted, so the code under test can proceed. A fake is a working implementation with a shortcut inside: an in-memory repository that really stores and retrieves, a payment gateway that really tracks balances but moves no money. Fakes have behavior; stubs have lines. A mock is a stub that also records how it was called, so the test can verify interactions afterwards. A spy wraps the real thing, records the calls, and lets the real behavior happen.

The selection logic follows from the jobs. Need a collaborator to merely exist? Dummy. Need it to answer predictably? Stub. Need it to behave, statefully, across a whole scenario? Fake. Need to prove your code called out correctly, a charge issued exactly once? Mock or spy.

Most suites need fakes and stubs constantly, mocks sparingly, and the vocabulary matters because 'mock everything' thinking collapses five tools into the one most prone to testing the test instead of the code.

We built an in-memory fake of our user repository for tests. How do we know the fake behaves like the real database repository and not like we imagine it does?

You stop trusting either implementation and write one contract suite that both must pass. The contract is a set of tests expressed purely in terms of the repository's interface and promises: saving a user and reading it back returns an equal user; finding by email is case-insensitive, if that's the promise; saving two users with the same email raises the duplicate error; updating changes the stored record; deleting removes it; queries return results in the documented order.

Then you run that identical suite twice, once wired to the fake, once wired to the real repository (against a throwaway database). Every test your unit suite writes against the fake is now implicitly backed: if the fake and the real thing both honor the contract, behavior verified against the fake transfers. When the real repository's behavior changes, a library upgrade alters its ordering, a migration changes a default, the contract run against the real thing fails and tells you the fake needs updating, instead of your whole suite silently testing a memory.

Two disciplines keep it honest. The contract may only assert documented promises, not accidents of the current database; if the contract needs a behavior, the interface owns it. And the fake should implement the contract in the simplest possible way, a dict and a list, because every cleverness in the fake is a place it can diverge.

This pattern, one contract, two implementations, is the general answer to 'is my double faithful', for repositories, gateways, queues, and file stores alike.

Twenty lines, and it's a genuine repository: it stores, it assigns ids, it enforces the duplicate-email rule, it normalizes case the way the real one does, and it answers lookups. Tests can drive whole scenarios against it, registration flows, duplicate handling, lookups, at memory speed with zero setup.

The size is the point. A fake earns trust by being too simple to hide divergence in: a dict, a counter, and the contract's rules written as plainly as possible. Every behavior the fake has should be traceable to a promise the real repository makes; the moment a fake grows query engines, transactions, or clever indexing 'for realism', it becomes a second product that needs its own tests.

Paired with a shared contract suite run against both this fake and the real repository, a double this small is enough to carry an entire unit-test suite. Small, faithful, and verified beats elaborate and assumed, every time.
Our fake payment gateway has grown to 800 lines with its own fee rules and refund logic. It basically reimplements the provider. Is that a problem, or just thoroughness?

It's a problem with a specific shape: you now maintain two payment systems, and only one of them processes money. Every rule in the fake is a claim about the provider, and claims maintained by hand drift. Worse, your tests now verify your checkout against your interpretation of the provider, formalized in 800 lines, so a misunderstanding gets tested as correct, at scale, with great confidence.

The line a fake should not cross is implementing policy that belongs to the other system. A healthy fake models the interface and the outcomes your code must handle: success, decline with a reason, timeout, duplicate submission, the shapes of responses. It should not model the provider's internal fee calculations or risk rules unless your code's behavior genuinely depends on them, and if it does, that dependence belongs behind a contract test against the real sandbox, because it's too important to fake.

The repair is subtraction. List every behavior the fake has; for each, ask which of your tests would change meaning if the behavior vanished. Delete what's left. Script outcomes rather than simulating causes: your checkout needs 'declined: insufficient funds' as a response, not a miniature bank deciding funds are insufficient.

A fake should be a stage set: convincing from the audience's side, plywood from behind. The moment it needs its own test suite, it has become a product, and a misleading one.
I need to test what our sync job does when the API fails halfway through, not on the first call but on like the seventh. Can a test double do that?

Yes, and this is one of the highest-value things doubles do, because mid-sequence failures are where data corruption lives and where real systems are hardest to rehearse against. The pattern is a scripted double: instead of answering the same way forever, it plays back a sequence you specify, six successes, then a failure, then whatever the retry should meet. Implementations vary from a list the double pops from, to a counter ('raise on call 7'), to a small script language, but the idea is constant: the failure's timing is part of the test's arrange step.

What you're really testing with that seventh-call failure is the job's memory and its conscience. Does it resume from the sixth item or restart and duplicate the first six? Does it report partial progress honestly, or claim success? Does the item that failed get retried, skipped, or silently dropped? Those behaviors are invisible to tests where the double fails immediately or never, which is why suites without scripted failures ship sync jobs whose recovery logic has literally never executed.

Build the capability once, as a reusable scripted double for each external boundary, and a whole category of scenarios becomes cheap: failure on the last call, failure then success on retry, alternating failures, a timeout after the server actually committed. The edge cases of distributed behavior are mostly just sequences, and sequences can be scripted.
