Each scenario is a one-line script change.

The production code had to earn this testability: it must take the clock and gateway as inputs rather than helping itself to the real ones. That's the recurring bargain of this whole discipline. Small seams at the boundaries, clocks and gateways passed in, buy you complete control of time and failure in tests, which is to say, control of the two things that make real systems hard to verify.
My team keeps saying 'contract tests' will keep our test doubles honest. What exactly is a contract test, and what should ours contain for our storage service wrapper?

A contract test is a suite that runs the same expectations against two implementations of one interface, the real thing and the double, so that 'the double behaves like reality' stops being an assumption and becomes a checked fact. For your storage wrapper, the contract is the list of promises your code actually relies on, stated once, executed twice.

For a storage service, a serious contract includes: saving an object and reading it back returns identical bytes; reading a missing key raises the documented not-found error, not an empty result; overwriting replaces completely; listing returns the keys under a prefix and only those; deleting a missing key behaves as documented, silently or with an error, whichever the wrapper promises; and metadata written at save time is readable at read time. Each promise becomes a test parameterized by implementation: run it against the real service (or its sandbox) in a slow, clearly-labeled job, and against the in-memory fake in the fast suite.

Three disciplines make or break it. The contract asserts only documented promises, never accidents of the current provider, or you'll cement quirks into your interface. The fake is maintained to the contract, not to the provider's full behavior; anything outside the contract is out of scope for the fake by definition. And the real-side run happens on a schedule and on provider upgrades, not just when someone remembers, because drift is a when, not an if.

When the contract run against reality fails while the fake stays green, you haven't got a nuisance; you've got the earliest possible warning that the ground moved, delivered by a test instead of a customer.
Someone suggested recording real API responses once and replaying them in tests ('cassettes'). What are the honest pros and cons?

The pros are real. Recorded responses are reality itself, not someone's memory of reality: the field names, the nesting, the odd nulls, the error payloads, all captured verbatim, so the whole class of 'the mock imagined the shape' bugs dies at the source. Recording is also fast to adopt; you wrap the HTTP layer, run the scenario once against the real service, and the fixture exists. And replay is deterministic and offline, so tests get the fidelity of integration with the speed of unit tests.

The cons are equally real. Cassettes age: the API evolves, the recording doesn't, and a suite replaying last year's responses is testing against a museum, so recordings need a refresh discipline and an owner. Recordings can leak: real responses contain real data, tokens, personal information, which must be scrubbed before the cassette enters the repo, and scrubbing must survive re-recording. Matching can be brittle: if the replay matches requests too literally, innocent changes, a new header, a reordered parameter, break tests that should pass; too loosely, and the wrong recording answers. And cassettes only cover interactions someone recorded; the unrecorded error path is as untested as ever.

The balanced verdict: cassettes are an excellent source of truth for building and refreshing hand-written fakes and stubs, and a reasonable replay mechanism for read-heavy integrations. They are not a substitute for a small set of live contract tests, because only a live test can tell you the recording and the reality have parted ways.
When a test fails I usually just scroll to see which test it was and start debugging the code. A senior dev told me I'm skipping the most informative step. What step?

Reading the failure message itself, slowly, as a diagnostic artifact, before touching the code. A good failure tells you four things in seconds: which behavior broke (the test's name), what was expected, what actually happened, and the values involved. The difference between expected and actual is frequently the whole diagnosis in embryo. Expected 270, got 260 is a ten-unit discrepancy with a shape: a missing item, a wrong discount, an unapplied fee, and each candidate can be checked against the test's inputs mentally before a debugger opens.

The habit to build is a small ritual. Read the test name as a sentence: the suite claims this behavior is broken. Read expected versus actual and compute the difference, the ratio, the pattern: off by one, off by a factor, off by exactly one element, completely different type. Ask whether the actual value looks like a neighboring behavior's correct answer, which would mean the code took the wrong path, or like this behavior computed with one step skipped. Only then open the code, and open it with a hypothesis already in hand.

Debugging from the code side first treats every failure as a search through everything. Debugging from the failure side treats it as evidence to be read. The second scales; the first doesn't survive a suite of five hundred tests.

The craft rule: an assert message should carry what a bug report needs, the inputs that produced the failure, the expected result, and the actual result, in the report's own words. Frameworks help: most assertion libraries produce this diff automatically for equality checks, which is one good reason to use their assert methods instead of the bare language assert. For computed checks, write the message as you go; it costs ten seconds while the context is in your head, and saves ten minutes later when it isn't.

Treat every assertion as a letter to the person who will read its failure at 2am. That person is you, and they deserve the evidence attached.

The better way is to assert in a form whose failure is a diff, not a wall. Equality between two collections is true or false; the useful information is entirely in how they differ, and set difference computes exactly that: what should be there and isn't, and what is there and shouldn't be. Each of those is a lead: missing items point at a filtering or loading bug, unexpected items point at contamination or an over-broad query.

Sometimes my test run shows a failure and the traceback points into my setup code, not the test itself or the code under test. Are those failures different in kind?

Completely different in kind, and confusing them wastes hours. A failure in the test body, at an assert, is the suite doing its job: a behavior claim was checked and found false. A failure in setup, an exception while building the world, means the test never ran at all. No claim was checked. The behavior might be fine, broken, or on fire; the run is silent about it, and the red mark against that test's name is a false accusation.

The diseases differ too. Setup failures are usually environmental or structural: a fixture that depends on leftover state, a factory broken by a model change, a shared resource that's exhausted, a file that a previous run left behind. The fix belongs in the fixture layer, and the blast radius is every test using that fixture, which is why one broken setup can paint fifty tests red while zero behaviors are broken.

Practical disciplines follow. Learn to read your runner's distinction between 'failures' and 'errors' if it makes one; errors are typically the setup kind. When a whole cluster of tests fails at once, suspect the shared setup before suspecting fifty behaviors. And keep setup code boring and defensive, because its failures are the least informative in the suite: they tell you the stage collapsed, nothing about the play.

Tests can be written to make this easy: include the inputs in the failure message, state the expected value's provenance ('policy: better single discount'), and where a pipeline exists, surface the intermediate totals. A test that shows its work turns debugging from archaeology into reading.
One of our tests fails 'sometimes' and the team calls it flaky, but I noticed the failures always involve totals ending in certain digits. Should I read anything into that?

Yes: a failure that correlates with the data is not flaky, it's a deterministic bug with a trigger nobody has named yet, and your observation is the first real clue. True flakiness correlates with time, order, load, or environment. Data-correlated failure correlates with the input's shape, which means there's a class of inputs the code handles wrongly, and the suite only samples that class occasionally.

Totals ending in certain digits points at the usual suspects in money code: rounding applied at the wrong stage (per line versus on the total), a comparison against a threshold that rounding nudges values across, or binary floating point making a total like 0.1 + 0.2 land a hair below a boundary it should sit on. Each hypothesis is testable in minutes once you have one failing input in hand.

So the workflow is: capture one failing case verbatim, inputs, seed, everything; reproduce it in isolation until it fails on demand; shrink it to the smallest input with the same failure; and only then read the code, with the trigger characterized. Then rename the test in your head from 'flaky' to 'the rounding-boundary bug', fix it, and keep the minimal case as a regression test.

The broader lesson is worth stating to your team: 'flaky' should be a conclusion reached after data-correlation has been ruled out, not a first impression. Half the flaky tests in most suites are real bugs wearing a disguise, and the disguise is removed by reading the failures instead of re-running them.
A test fails with 'expected 42, got None' and there's no stack trace or error anywhere. The function under test returns None instead of crashing. How do I debug a failure with no evidence?

buggy version returns: None -> test says 'expected 42, got None', no trace
fixed version raises:   ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero  (the actual bug, in plain sight)

A failure with no evidence is itself the evidence: something between the error and the test is eating exceptions. The function wraps its work in a blanket try/except and converts every failure, typo, bad input, division by zero, into a silent None. The test then compares 42 against None and reports a mismatch that contains zero information about the cause, because the cause was deliberately destroyed at the scene.

The debugging move is to remove the burial, temporarily or permanently: let the exception propagate and the real error appears with its type, message, and traceback, here a plain division by zero that takes ten seconds to understand. What was an archaeology expedition becomes a reading exercise.

The design lesson is one of the most valuable in all of testing-adjacent code: broad exception swallowing doesn't make code robust, it makes failures undiagnosable, converting loud, located errors into silent, distant wrong values. Code that catches everything should at minimum log the exception with its traceback. And when you inherit a 'got None' failure, your first suspect is never the arithmetic. It's the handler standing between the arithmetic and you, holding a shovel.
Test failures come with a wall of stack trace, dozens of frames of framework code. How do experienced devs read those without going cross-eyed?

They don't read the wall; they scan it with a filter. A test traceback has three strata. The bottom frames are the test framework starting the test, pure plumbing, almost never relevant. The top frame is where the failure was raised, an assert or an exception, which tells you the failure's type and message. And somewhere in the middle are your frames: your test, and the code under test, the only frames where the bug can live.

The reading method is: start at the failure line itself, the exception type and message, because that's the summary. Then scan upward from the bottom of your code's involvement, find the deepest frame that is yours, the innermost call into your code, and read that line: it's the exact statement executing when things went wrong, and its local values, if the runner shows them, are the scene of the crime. Framework frames between your frames are just the corridor; walk through, don't dust them for prints.

Two more habits help. Learn your framework's way of collapsing or hiding its own frames; most runners have a verbosity or traceback style setting, and choosing the short style is a one-time fix for the wall. And when the trace shows the failure raised inside a library you call, the question to carry into debugging is not 'what's wrong with the library' but 'what did my frame hand it', because the answer is nearly always there.

A stack trace is a story told from the scene backwards. Read the last page first, then only your own chapters.

Nothing is wrong with your code; something is wrong with the test's model of numbers. 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so their sum is the nearest representable double, which prints as 0.30000000000000004. Exact equality compares bit patterns, and the pattern for the computed sum differs from the pattern for the literal 0.3 by one part in about 10^16. The failure message was telling the truth at a precision the domain doesn't care about.

The reading skill is recognizing this species on sight: when expected and actual agree to fifteen significant digits and differ in the sixteenth, you are looking at representation noise, not a logic bug, and no amount of staring at the addition will find a defect that isn't there.

The fix is to assert at the precision the domain means. For floats generally, a closeness assertion with an explicit tolerance, as shown. For money specifically, the deeper fix is to stop letting floats carry currency: compute in integer cents or a decimal type, where 10 + 20 is exactly 30 and equality is honest again. The test failure, read correctly, was a design review of your numeric types, delivered by the suite for free.
Our bug reports from QA are usually vague ('discount seems wrong sometimes'), but our own failing tests feel different when I read them. Can a test failure actually serve as a good bug report?

A well-built failing test is close to the perfect bug report, because it contains, in executable form, every element a vague report lacks. It has exact reproduction steps: the arrange section is the setup, the act is the trigger, no 'sometimes', no missing context, it fails on demand every time. It has a precise statement of expected versus actual behavior, with concrete values. It has scope: the test's name states the one behavior that's broken, and the rest of the suite passing bounds the blast radius. And it has a built-in verification: the fix is done when this turns green without breaking its neighbors.

Compare 'discount seems wrong sometimes'. No inputs, no expected value, no frequency, no way to know when it's fixed. Converting that report into a failing test is not bureaucratic overhead before the real work; in most cases it is the majority of the debugging, because pinning the reproduction and the expectation is where the understanding happens.

This suggests a workflow worth adopting as a team norm: bugs enter as failing tests, written from the report plus one round of questions, before fixes are attempted. The failing test is the shared, unambiguous statement of the problem that the reporter, the fixer, and the reviewer can all point at. And it never leaves: after the fix it's the regression test, so the bug report becomes the permanent guard against its own return. Vague reports evaporate after a fix. Tests stay on duty.
Our dashboard says the codebase has 90% test coverage. The team treats that as '90% tested'. What does the number actually mean, and what doesn't it mean?

It means that when the test suite runs, 90% of the counted units, usually lines or statements, get executed at least once. That is all it has ever meant, and the gap between that and 'tested' is where overconfidence lives.

Execution is not verification. A line can run under a test that asserts nothing about its result, or asserts something so loose the line could return garbage and pass. Coverage also can't see what's missing: the requirement nobody implemented has no lines, so it contributes no uncovered red; the error branch that exists but is never triggered does show up, but the input class nobody thought of leaves no trace in the metric at all. And the number is an average that hides distribution: 90% overall can mean the payment path is at 40% while getters and configuration are at a padded 100%.

Used well, coverage is a floor-detector and a gap-finder: sort by least-covered files, look at which lines never run, and ask of each, 'is this dead, or is this the error path we never test?' Those are valuable questions. Used as a quality score or a target to hit, it actively misleads, because the cheapest way to raise it is to execute code without checking behavior, which makes the suite look stronger as it gets weaker.

Report coverage to find holes. Never report it as a verdict.

Mutation testing inverts the usual question. Instead of asking 'does my code pass my tests', it asks 'would my tests notice if the code were wrong?' A tool, or here a human, makes one small change to the code, a flipped comparison, a swapped operator, an off-by-one constant, creating a mutant, and runs the suite. If some test fails, the mutant is killed: the suite was watching that behavior. If every test passes, the mutant survives, and a survivor is an indictment: there is a real behavioral change your suite cannot see.

Your original suite has a survivor, and the survivor is instructive. The tests at 90 and 150 sit in the interiors of the two classes, where `>=` and `>` agree. The single added test at the boundary value 100, the exact point where the operators disagree, kills the mutant instantly.

You don't need tooling to use this idea weekly. Pick the riskiest function you touched, hand-make two or three plausible mutants, an off-by-one, a negated condition, a wrong constant, and run your tests. Every survivor is a precisely located hole in your suite, described in the most actionable form possible: 'this specific wrongness is invisible to us'.
Line coverage, branch coverage, behavior coverage: our tool reports the first, our lead talks about the third. What's the actual difference?

They measure three different things, in ascending order of meaning and descending order of measurability.

Line coverage asks: did this line execute during the suite? It's easy to count and easy to game, because a line can execute under a test that asserts nothing about it.

Branch coverage asks: did each decision go both ways? Every if taken true and false, every loop entered and skipped, every fallback used. It's stricter: code can have every line executed while a branch outcome, say the false side of a condition guarding an error path, never occurs, because some other route reached the same lines. Branch gaps are usually where untested error handling hides.

Behavior coverage asks: of the behaviors the system promises its users, how many are pinned by a test that would fail if the behavior changed? This is the one your lead cares about, and no tool can count it, because the denominator, the set of promised behaviors, lives in requirements and people's heads, not in the code. A function can be at 100% line and branch coverage while an entire promised behavior, the discount also applying to gift cards, has no lines yet and therefore no coverage signal at all.

Use the tool's numbers to find unexecuted code. Use behavior thinking, a list of promises with a test beside each, to find untested commitments. The second list is shorter, harder to build, and the only one that means 'tested' in the sense users care about.

A pile of killed mutants across the plausible wrongnesses is what 'this behavior is actually protected' means, in a way a coverage percentage never quite says.

But no, a survivor is not always a test problem, and chasing every survivor will teach you the exceptions. Some mutants are equivalent: the changed code behaves identically to the original for every possible input (swapping the order of independent statements, replacing `>=` with `>` plus an adjusted constant done consistently), and no test can kill an equivalent mutant, because there's nothing to detect. Some survivors live in code whose behavior genuinely doesn't matter, dead paths, cosmetic ordering. And some survivors point at the code, not the tests: a branch so convoluted that no one can state its intended behavior has a specification problem wearing a testing costume.

So the workflow is triage, not extermination. For each survivor ask: could a user tell the difference between the original and this mutant? If yes, write the test that tells it. If no, note it as equivalent or irrelevant and move on. The mutation score that matters is not 100%; it's 'no survivable mutant changes anything a user can observe'.
Our payment module shows 96% line coverage, yet a bug in the payment-failure path reached production last month. How can both be true?

Easily, and the anatomy is worth understanding because this exact pattern repeats everywhere. Line coverage is an average over the whole module, and a payment module is mostly happy-path machinery: request building, response parsing, success handling, receipts, logging. If all of that is well tested, it contributes hundreds of covered lines. The failure path, the decline handling, the timeout handler, the retry logic, might be thirty lines. Thirty uncovered lines in a module of eight hundred is a rounding error in the percentage and the entire risk profile of the system.

There's a second mechanism too: the failure path's lines can be technically covered while its behavior is unverified. A test that triggers a decline and asserts only 'does not crash' executes the failure lines and checks almost nothing about them; the wrong retry count, the missing customer notification, the incorrectly recorded status all pass. Coverage counts execution, not assertion.

The fixes are about aiming rather than volume. Read coverage as a per-branch list of what never runs, and weight it by fear: error paths, fallbacks, and recovery code get tested first, because they run rarely, under stress, when the user is already having a bad day. For the critical paths, add the mutation habit: deliberately break the failure handling, swap the retry count, drop the notification, and check the suite notices. A module whose failure paths are both executed and asserted is protected in the way the 96% figure only pretends to describe.
There's a whole 'new checkout' path in our code that I suspect no test has ever run. How would I confirm that suspicion?

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
Suspicion confirmed, and the method generalizes: instrument the paths (here by hand, in real life with your coverage tool), run the suite, and ask which named regions never executed. The new checkout path has literally never run under a test, because the flag that gates it is false in every configuration the tests load. It could contain a syntax-valid, completely broken implementation, and the suite would be green forever.

Dead and dormant code corrupts testing in two directions. It drags the coverage number down, which teams then chase by writing meaningless tests for code that shouldn't exist. And while it sits there, it rots against every refactor of the shared code around it, so the day someone flips the flag in production, they activate the least-maintained code in the repository, under real traffic, with no test ever having stood on it.

The resolution is a decision, not a test. If the new path is the future, it needs its flag exercised in tests now, with the path held to the same standard as the live one. If it's abandoned, delete it; version control remembers it better than the codebase does. What you can't defend is the middle state: shipped, reachable by configuration, and verified by nothing.
Can I get a 'mutation score' for a small module by hand, to see how strong the suite really is? Walk me through what it would show.

arguments.code:
def add_tax(price):      return round(price * 1.08, 2)
def bulk_discount(qty):  return 0.10 if qty >= 10 else 0.0
def clamp_score(s):      return max(0, min(100, s))

def suite(fns):
    tax, bulk, clamp = fns
    return all([
        tax(100) == 108.00,
        bulk(10) == 0.10,
        bulk(3) == 0.0,
        clamp(120) == 100,
        clamp(50) == 50,
    ])

MUTANTS = {
    "M1 tax rate 1.08 -> 1.06": (
        lambda p: round(p * 1.06, 2), bulk_discount, clamp_score),
    "M2 bulk >= 10 -> > 10": (
        add_tax, lambda q: 0.10 if q > 10 else 0.0, clamp_score),
    "M3 clamp cap 100 -> 90": (
        add_tax, bulk_discount, lambda s: max(0, min(90, s))),
    "M4 clamp floor 0 -> -10": (
        add_tax, bulk_discount, lambda s: max(-10, min(100, s))),
}
killed = 0
for name, fns in MUTANTS.items():
    dead = not suite(fns)
    killed += dead
    print(f"{name}: {'KILLED' if dead else 'SURVIVED'}")
print(f"mutation score: {killed}/{len(MUTANTS)}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
M1 tax rate 1.08 -> 1.06: KILLED
M2 bulk >= 10 -> > 10: KILLED
M3 clamp cap 100 -> 90: KILLED
M4 clamp floor 0 -> -10: SURVIVED
mutation score: 3/4

The score is 3 of 4, and the survivor is the deliverable. M1, the tax-rate change, is killed by the tax test. M2, the off-by-one on the bulk threshold, is killed by the test standing exactly on 10. M3, the lowered cap, is killed by the test at 120. M4 survives: the suite never tests a negative score, so lowering the floor to -10 changes nothing any test can see. The suite's blind spot is now named with surgical precision: clamp_score's lower bound is unverified, and a negative score would flow downstream instead of being clamped to zero.

Notice how much more actionable this is than a coverage report on the same module, which would show every line executed and report 100%. Line coverage asks whether code ran. Mutation asks whether anyone would notice if it were wrong, which is the question 'is this tested' actually means.

By hand, this is an afternoon's technique: take the riskiest module, write four to six plausible one-line corruptions (operators, constants, conditions, dropped calls), and run the suite against each. Every survivor converts directly into a test to write. Tooling automates the corruption at scale, but the insight per survivor is identical.
Leadership wants 100% coverage and has made it a team goal. As the person who'll have to get there, what should I expect and what should I push back on?

Expect the first 80% to be the valuable part and the last 20% to be increasingly expensive theater, and plan your pushback around that asymmetry. The climb to high coverage forces tests onto error paths and forgotten modules, which is genuinely good. The final stretch is dominated by code that is disproportionately hard to test and disproportionately unimportant when tested: defensive branches for impossible states, framework glue, simple accessors, error handlers for errors that cannot be triggered from outside, and the occasional module everyone is afraid to touch, now wrapped in tests that assert nothing but execute everything, written solely to move the number.

That's the corruption to push back on: a hard 100% target doesn't measure testing quality, it purchases its own gaming. Suites bloat with assertion-free executions, brittle tests of implementation details, and mocks of everything, and the suite gets slower and less trusted as the number gets prettier.

The counter-offer that usually lands: coverage as a floor and a ratchet, not a target. No file's coverage may fall; new code arrives with its behaviors tested; and instead of a global percentage, name the critical modules, payments, auth, data writes, and hold those to behavior-level standards verified with spot mutation checks. Offer leadership the metric that answers their real question, 'would we catch a serious regression before customers do', in the form they can audit: a list of the system's critical behaviors, each with its protecting test.

If the 100% mandate stands anyway, negotiate the exclusions in writing: generated code, configuration, trivial accessors, and defensive dead branches. A 100% with honest exclusions is achievable and mostly harmless. A 100% without them is a tax on every future change, paid in suite maintenance, forever.

My coverage tool says a function is at 100%, but I have a nagging feeling one case is untested. The function is a bouncer check: adults with a ticket get in. What case could hide under 100% line coverage?

arguments.code:
def check(age, has_ticket, hits):
    adult = age >= 18
    hits.add(f"age>=18 evaluated -> {adult}")
    if not adult:
        return False
    hits.add(f"has_ticket evaluated -> {has_ticket}")
    return has_ticket

hits = set()
print("test 1 (adult with ticket): ", check(20, True, hits))
print("test 2 (minor with ticket): ", check(16, True, hits))
print("branch outcomes exercised:  ", sorted(hits))
print("never exercised:             has_ticket evaluated -> False")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
test 1 (adult with ticket):  True
test 2 (minor with ticket):  False
branch outcomes exercised:   ['age>=18 evaluated -> False', 'age>=18 evaluated -> True', 'has_ticket evaluated -> True']
never exercised:             has_ticket evaluated -> False

Your nagging feeling is correct, and the hidden case is the most important one the bouncer has: an adult without a ticket. Watch the mechanics. The function is tiny and both its return paths execute under the two tests, so line coverage honestly reports 100%. But the second condition, has_ticket, is only ever evaluated when the first is true, thanks to short-circuiting, and the only test that reaches it has a ticket. The outcome 'ticket evaluated and found false' never occurs in the suite, which means the behavior 'adult without a ticket is turned away' is entirely unverified. If the return were wired wrong for exactly that case, nothing would catch it.

This is the difference between line coverage and branch coverage made concrete. Lines are places; branches are outcomes of decisions, and a decision with two conditions has outcomes that no single line reveals. The instrumentation here, recording each condition's evaluated result, is what branch and condition coverage tools automate.

The durable lesson: for any condition guarding something that matters, enumerate its outcomes, including the ones short-circuiting hides, and make sure a test stands on each. The case most likely to be missing is the one where an early condition passes and a later one fails, because writing it requires imagining partial success, and partial success is where real users live.
People say 'tests are documentation'. Honestly, when I join a project I read the README and the code. Should I be reading the tests instead?

Read the tests first, because they're the only documentation that is guaranteed to be current. A README describes the system as someone hoped it would be, on the day they wrote it. Code describes what the system does, including its accidents and workarounds, with no marking of which parts are intentional. Tests, when they're any good, describe what the system is supposed to do, behavior by behavior, in executable form, and they cannot silently rot: the day a documented behavior stops being true, its test turns red and someone must either fix the code or deliberately change the test, which is a recorded decision.

Practically, a well-kept suite answers the questions a new hire actually has faster than any prose. What does this module promise? The test names list it. What does a valid order look like? The factories show one. What happens on a declined card? There's a named test with the expected outcome. What are the edge cases the team has been burned by? They're the regression tests, each one a scar with a story.

The caveat is that this only holds for suites written as specifications: behavior-named tests, realistic factories, expectations from requirements. A suite of implementation-mirroring tests documents the code's wiring, which the code already documents. So yes, read the tests first, and if they're unreadable as documentation, that's not a reading failure. It's the suite's first bug report.
Our test names are things like test_checkout_2 and test_discount_case_b. Does naming really matter that much?

More than almost anything else in the suite, because the name is the part of the test everyone reads and the only part visible in a failure list. When a build breaks at 2am, the first information anyone gets is a list of names. 'test_discount_case_b failed' says nothing; the responder must open the test, read its body, and reconstruct what behavior is at stake. 'Member discount does not stack with a coupon' failed is the diagnosis's first sentence, readable from the CI summary on a phone.

Good test names state the behavior and the condition, in the vocabulary of the business, not the code: 'trial users cannot download reports', 'orders over $75 ship free', 'a second refund on the same order is rejected'. Read in sequence, the names form the specification of the module, which is why the tests-as-documentation idea stands or falls on naming.

Naming is also a design instrument while you write. If you cannot name the test in one business sentence, you usually don't yet know what behavior you're testing, and the test you're about to write will be vague in exactly the same way. Struggle with the name first; the test gets clearer when the sentence does.

Rename the existing ones opportunistically, a few whenever you touch a file. It's the cheapest large improvement a suite can receive.
Surely not everything deserves a test. Where do experienced testers deliberately NOT write tests?

Several places, and naming them protects the suite's credibility, because tests written for worthless targets cost maintenance and return nothing.

Trivial accessors and assignments: a getter that returns a field, a setter that stores it, a constructor that copies parameters. There's no behavior to protect; the test would restate the line it tests. Code you don't own: the framework's routing, the standard library's sort, your ORM's basic persistence. Testing those verifies other people's products and breaks on their upgrades. Pure configuration and data: the list of country codes, the tax table's contents. Those need review and validation, maybe a schema check, not unit tests per value. One-off glue with no logic: a script that passes arguments through unchanged.

And the subtle one: behavior that is about to be deleted or is explicitly experimental behind a flag, where the honest move is a note and a date, not a suite.

The principle tying these together: a test earns its place by protecting a behavior whose breakage would hurt and whose correctness isn't guaranteed by something simpler. Where breakage is impossible, impossible to detect, or someone else's problem, the test is ceremony. Spend the effort where the risk is: the rules, the money, the state transitions, the boundaries.

I refactored a queue class from a list to a deque for performance and not one test broke, even though I changed every method's internals. My coworker says that's suspicious, the tests must be too weak. Who's right?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
list-backed  -> ['first', 'second', 1, 'third']
deque-backed -> ['first', 'second', 1, 'third']

You are, and the run shows why. The tests exercise the queue's contract: items come out in arrival order, the length tracks what's inside. Both implementations, the list with its expensive front-pop and the deque built for it, satisfy that contract identically, so the suite is green across a total internal replacement. That is not weakness; that is the definition of testing behavior instead of implementation. The suite cannot tell the two classes apart because, from every caller's perspective, there is nothing to tell apart.

Your coworker's suspicion would be justified if the tests had asserted on the internals: that the backing store is a list, that pop calls a particular method, that items live at specific indexes. Those tests would have broken during your refactor while the behavior stayed perfect, and they would have taught the team that refactoring is punished, which is how codebases fossilize.

The general principle is worth stating as a rule: a test should be incapable of distinguishing between two correct implementations of the same contract. If it can distinguish them, it's testing the implementation, and it will levy a tax on every future improvement. When a refactor breaks tests, the first question is never 'how do I fix the tests'. It's 'did the behavior change, or did the tests overreach'. Here, the silence of the suite is the sound of it doing its job.
I wrote a test that verifies my checkout calls the pricing service exactly twice. My lead made me delete it. The information seemed useful though. Why was she right?

Because 'calls the pricing service exactly twice' is not a behavior your users or callers care about; it's a fact about the current implementation's choreography, and it will change the moment anyone optimizes, caches, batches, or inlines the pricing, all without the checkout's actual behavior changing at all. Your test would fail on each of those improvements, announcing a breakage that didn't happen.

Tests like this invert the suite's purpose. Instead of standing guard over what the system owes, they stand guard over how the system currently happens to work, and the team pays for the guard twice: once when the brittle test breaks spuriously, and again in the refactoring that never happens because someone looks at the wall of red it would cause and quietly chooses not to improve the code.

The useful information inside your test deserves a fair hearing, though. If the concern was performance, two calls being a budget, the honest test measures the budget: time the checkout, or count calls at the system boundary against a documented limit, with the limit in the test's name. If the concern was correctness, that the right prices were used, the honest test asserts the total. Either way, the assertion lands on an outcome someone can defend in a sentence.

A good deletion question for any test: if this fails next year, will the responder thank it or curse it? Interaction-count tests on internal calls are cursed almost every time.
Everyone cites the 'test pyramid': many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end. For a small codebase like ours, is that real advice or big-company folklore?

It's real advice with a practical core that survives scaling down, though the proportions matter less than the reasoning. The pyramid isn't a quota; it's a cost curve. Unit tests are fast, precise about what broke, and cheap to write for logic. Integration tests verify that components actually cooperate, which unit tests structurally cannot see, but they're slower and their failures need more interpretation. End-to-end tests prove the whole system works from the user's seat, and they're the slowest, flakiest, and vaguest about causes. A healthy suite buys verification in bulk at the cheap layers and spends sparingly at the expensive one.

For a small codebase, the honest translation is: put most of your effort into fast tests around the rules and calculations, because that's where your bugs will be. Keep a handful of integration tests over the real seams, your API against a real database, your checkout against a fake gateway, because seams are where assumptions go to die. And keep a very small number of end-to-end smoke paths, the three or four journeys the business cannot afford to have broken, run as a final check.

Where small teams go wrong is inverting the pyramid because end-to-end tests feel most convincing, then living with a suite that takes twenty minutes, flakes weekly, and reports failures like 'checkout is broken somewhere'. The pyramid is just the discipline of asking, for each behavior: what's the cheapest test that would catch this being wrong? Answer that per behavior and the pyramid builds itself.
Deleting tests feels wrong, like removing a smoke detector. Are there tests that should actually be deleted?

Yes, and keeping them isn't caution; it's hoarding, with the same result: the valuable things get buried. Four categories earn deletion. Tests of behavior that no longer exists: the feature was removed, but its tests were kept 'just in case', and now they constrain nothing except refactorings. Duplicates: three tests that exercise the same behavior through the same path with trivially different data, where one well-chosen case carries all the information; keep the clearest, delete the echoes. Tests that assert implementation details of a refactored design, where the behavior is already covered at the contract level; these don't protect anything the contract tests don't, and they tax every change. And tests that have been failing or skipped for so long that the team routes around them; a permanently red or ignored test is worse than none, because it trains everyone to disregard the suite's signals.

The smoke detector analogy actually supports deletion when applied precisely: you remove the detector that chirps randomly every night, because it's teaching the household to ignore detectors, and you replace it or fix the cause. What you never delete is a test protecting live behavior merely because it's inconvenient, slow, or currently failing against a real bug. The question is always whether the test still guards a promise someone relies on. If the promise is gone, the guard is litter. If the promise lives, the test stays, and gets repaired instead.
Our suite takes 25 minutes and developers have stopped running it locally. The tests themselves seem fine individually. Is slowness really a testing problem and not just a CI problem?

It's a testing problem, because a suite's value is realized at the moment a developer runs it, and a 25-minute suite has quietly resigned from that job. What replaces it is worse than no suite: developers batch changes and run it rarely, so failures arrive in bundles of five commits and the 'which change broke it' question gets expensive; or they run only the file they touched, and cross-module regressions sail to CI; or the suite becomes a ceremony performed by the build server while local development proceeds unguarded. The feedback loop that makes tests worth writing, change code, see the verdict in seconds, has been severed.

The causes are usually design, not hardware. Tests that boot the whole application to check a calculation. Integration tests wearing unit-test clothing, hitting real databases and networks for logic that could be checked in memory. Setup that rebuilds the world from scratch for every test when a transaction rollback would do. A few sociopathic tests, the sleep, the giant import, the full-table seed, contributing half the runtime between them. Profile the suite the way you'd profile the application: the distribution is almost always a long tail plus a few whales.

The standard to defend: the fast suite, the one developers run constantly, should complete in the time a person can hold their attention, well under a minute for the unit layer, with slower integration and end-to-end layers running in CI on their own schedules. Speed is not a luxury feature of a test suite. It's the property that determines whether the suite exists in practice or only in the repository.
I've inherited a legacy module with no tests that everyone is afraid to change, and now it has to change. Writing tests for behavior I don't understand feels impossible. Where do I start?

With characterization tests, which invert the usual contract. A normal test asserts what the code should do. A characterization test asserts what the code currently does, whatever that is, because your first job is not to judge the behavior but to pin it down so that change becomes observable. You run the module against varied, realistic inputs, record its actual outputs, and encode those as tests. Some of what you record will be bugs. You pin them anyway, with a comment saying so, because right now the goal is a safety net, not a verdict.

The craft is in the input selection. Use production-shaped data, real examples from logs and the database, plus the boundary values of every range you can find in the code. You're building a tripwire field around current behavior: after your change, any output that differs is a difference you must be able to explain, intended or accidental. That transforms refactoring from 'edit and pray' into 'edit and review the diffs', which is the entire game with legacy code.

Then change the code in small steps, the smallest refactorings you can name, running the characterization suite after each. Where a pinned behavior turns out to be a bug the business wants fixed, fix it deliberately, update that one test, and let the commit record the decision.

Two warnings. Don't try to understand everything first; characterization is how you earn understanding safely, by experiment rather than by reading. And don't skip the ugly inputs: legacy modules are most dangerous exactly where their behavior is strangest, and those are the cases your net most needs to hold.

Capstone question: I'm designing the test plan for a small checkout module (cart totals, one discount rule, a payment gateway, a receipt email). Lay out what you'd actually test, and just as importantly, what you'd leave out.

Start from the promises, because the plan is the promise list with a test beside each. Cart totals: subtotal arithmetic on empty, single, and many-item carts, with the rounding rule pinned at the cent level, integer cents if the module allows it. The discount rule: each equivalence class (no code, member, student, invalid), the boundary of any threshold in it, and the interaction the business cares most about, whether discounts stack, stated as one named test. Money seams: totals exactly at the free-shipping or discount thresholds, a cent above and below.

The gateway gets a fake, scripted: success confirms the order and stores the charge id; decline leaves the order unpaid with the right customer message; timeout produces the unknown state and, critically, no blind retry, tested by asserting the gateway saw exactly one charge attempt. The email gets a recording stub: exactly one receipt, right recipient, right total in the body. A few properties patrol broadly: the total is never negative, never exceeds the subtotal without a stated reason, and applying the same discount twice changes nothing the second time if the rule says so.

Integration earns a thin layer: the module against the real repository and the gateway's sandbox, run in CI, asserting the contract, not the details. End-to-end gets exactly one journey: a standard purchase, happy path, as a smoke bell.

Now the omissions, which are half the craft. No tests of the gateway library's internals, the email provider's rendering, or the framework's routing. No interaction-count tests on internal calls. No test per tax-table row; a schema validation and three boundary rows carry it. No end-to-end matrix of every discount against every payment outcome; that cross-product lives at the unit layer where it's fast, and the single smoke journey proves the wires connect. The plan's shape is the pyramid with a spine: many fast behavior tests, scripted doubles at the two external seams, properties on the money invariants, and a deliberate, written list of what is not tested and why. That last list is what separates a test plan from a pile of tests.
